discussion_comments.comment_body: @Biki-das Is it possible to re-use the approach from https://github.com/react/react/pull/35723, where we read from profiler store?

I tried using the profiler-store approach, but it doesn't seem to capture this case because it's exercising a different code path than #35723.

That PR fixed entries in `recordProfilingDurations`/`didFiberRender`, which is what the flamegraph (`didRender`) uses. The issue I'm fixing is only in the trace-updates highlight overlay (`traceNearestHostComponentUpdate` in `mountFiberRecursively`), so the profiler logic never changes.

For a re-mount, `recordProfilingDurations` sees `prevFiber == null` and correctly records `didRender: true`, which means the flamegraph looks exactly the same with or without my change. Because of that, a profiler-store assertion can't distinguish the fixed behavior from the broken one.

Subscribing to the `traceUpdates` event lets me verify the actual overlay output, which is the behavior that's changing. If there's a better seam to test the overlay directly, I'm happy to use that instead.
@Biki-das Which test in this suite currently fails on main branch without your changes?

`does not highlight a component when its filtered ancestor re-mounts` is the only test that fails on `main` (the re-mounted host gets highlighted) and passes with the fix.

The other two already pass on `main`. I added them to lock in the behavior that shouldn't change: genuine re-renders and first-time mounts should still be highlighted. An earlier version of my fix was too aggressive and ended up suppressing the new-content case, so these tests guard against that regression.

I'm happy to remove them or mark them as characterization tests if you'd prefer to keep only the regression test.

Instead of eventLog approach cleaner to use same approach as in https://github.com/Omcodes23/react/blob/d951652f9ddf036f61d0ecea89caca9188f9160f/packages/react-dom/src/__tests__/DOMPropertyOperations-test.js#L284 (`jest.fn` + related assertions). Same in other tests.
I would appreciate if you can carefully go through all the AI generated code yourself before asking for review. For instance these are not used at all. What is the purpose for these?

This test was manually written to cover a specific gap. I hand-crafted the custom property setter scenario because it addresses a real hydration concern that wasn't being tested:

- Custom elements often use property setters for internal state, not just attributes
- The fix in ReactDOMComponent.js calls setPropOnCustomElement() for each prop
- But was it actually triggering property setters? No test verified this

So I deliberately designed this test structure:
1. Create a custom element with a property backed by an internal field (_internalValue)
2. Check pre-hydration state (property = "unset", untouched)
3. Hydrate with customProperty="hydrated-value" 
4. Assert the setter actually ran (customProperty and _internalValue now = "hydrated-value")

This is intentional, not generated. The test proves our fix works end-to-end for properties, not just attributes. Commit: 64e57d7d0.

Let's use Jest's `spyOn` so that 'jest.restoreAllMocks' just works.

Otherwise we might accidentally leak further than intended depending on the Jest runner and environment setup.
we should use `assertConsoleErrorDev` instead.
Updated — the test now uses assertConsoleErrorDev instead of manually spying on console.error.

Nit: could also use a test asserting that warning does not fire on correct usage, though thats likely covered by other `use` tests. And maybe rerender this at the end to make sure warning doesn't fire again.

> could also use a test asserting that warning does not fire on correct usage

That would be complicated, because our gating mechanism for tests asserts that any test run that doesn't pass the check should fail. In other words, the base scenario should fail, but this won't be true for the behavior that will be tested.
Actually, I could just remove these gating conditions
We should list to whatever this is module calling. Intercepting module internals should be a last resort.
Updated the test to listen for the browser-level `error` event and assert its public payload instead of mocking `shared/reportGlobalError`.

We've held back on unit tests very well over the past years. This test is just verbatim repeating the implmentation and will just be an obstacle for any future refactor.

DevTools regression test already cover multiple versions so this doesn't seem to add new coverage.
Removed.
Can you use `assertConsoleErrorDev` instead?

No, because I am patching a console not to just intercept the message, but to wait for the specific console.error call, pass the test and avoid being stuck in an infinite loop.

I could use `assertConsoleErrorDev` to validate that the message was logged, but waiting for the message already implies that check.
Can you use `utils.actAsync` here? This should also allow removing the Promise on line 632.

Does it have to be async, though? Does it fail if you check it synchronously? 

If it fails, can you try emitting the event as part of `act` or `actAsync`?
```
utils.act(() => ownerWindow.dispatchEvent(keyEvent));
```
